query: Given a CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy where conventional casting yields porosity and a homogeneous but soft single-phase structure, and where previous attempts suffered from low hardness, propose a solid-state processing strategy involving high-energy milling followed by rapid sintering. The target is to suppress porosity while driving the formation of a fine-grained nanocrystalline solid solution (dominated by FCC with minor BCC) rather than a brittle HCP phase often associated with Titanium-rich systems. Incorporate known constraints on displacement rates and thermal expansion during sintering into the hypothesis. Define the operating regime (temperature/strain rate) where this dual-phase stability is maximized, and propose a specific mechanical test (e.g., indentation load and dwell time) that would falsify the claim that the observed hardness is due to grain refinement rather than solute strengthening.

generation.hypothesis: High-energy ball milling of CoCrFeNiTi elemental powders followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 950°C with a heating rate of 100°C/min and a holding time of 5 minutes under 60 MPa uniaxial pressure will suppress porosity and stabilize a fine-grained (approx. 50-100 nm) nanocrystalline FCC solid solution with a minor BCC phase, while kinetically suppressing the formation of the brittle HCP Ti-rich phase and preventing excessive grain growth.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental powder mixture of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti with a stoichiometric ratio of 1:1:1:1:1, exhibiting high surface energy and potential oxide layers.
generation.intervention: Mechanical alloying via high-energy ball milling for 10 hours in an argon atmosphere, followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 950°C with a heating rate of 100°C/min and a holding time of 5 minutes under 60 MPa uniaxial pressure.
generation.conditions: Atmosphere: High-purity Argon (O2 < 10 ppm); Pressure: 60 MPa; Heating rate: 100°C/min; Dwell time: 5 min; Temperature: 950°C (approx. 0.6 Tm).
generation.structural_mediator: Severe plastic deformation induced by milling creates a high density of dislocations and nanoscale mixing, while the rapid thermal cycle of SPS utilizes the stored deformation energy to drive solid-state diffusion and grain boundary migration without allowing sufficient time for the thermodynamically favored HCP phase to nucleate and grow.
generation.mechanism: The rapid heating rate (100°C/min) and short dwell time (5 min) in SPS exceed the critical nucleation rate for the HCP phase but are sufficient to activate diffusion for the formation of the metastable FCC/BCC solid solution. The high uniaxial pressure (60 MPa) ensures pore closure (suppressing porosity) and enhances atomic mobility via pressure-assisted diffusion, while the high strain rate during the initial sintering stage (thermal expansion mismatch between Ti and other elements) generates local stress fields that stabilize the FCC lattice against the HCP transformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A fully dense (>98% theoretical density) nanocrystalline alloy with a grain size of 50-100 nm, consisting of a dominant FCC phase with a minor BCC phase, exhibiting a Vickers hardness of 450-550 HV, significantly higher than the cast material but lower than a fully martensitic or HCP-dominated structure.
generation.baseline: Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi alloy, which exhibits porosity, a coarse-grained single-phase FCC structure, and low hardness (approx. 150-200 HV).
generation.boundary: The strategy is valid only if the milling time is sufficient to achieve extreme nanocrystallinity but not so long as to induce excessive cold welding or contamination (e.g., carbides/oxides) that prevents sintering; the SPS temperature must remain below 1050°C to avoid grain coarsening and HCP precipitation, and above 850°C to ensure sufficient diffusion.
generation.uncertainty: There is a risk that the specific Ti content (20 at.%) may still drive local HCP nucleation at grain boundaries despite the rapid kinetics, potentially leading to a slight reduction in ductility or localized brittleness not captured by bulk hardness measurements. Additionally, the exact critical heating rate to suppress HCP may vary based on the specific milling media and initial oxide content, and contamination from milling media (e.g., carbides) may occur if milling exceeds 10 hours.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform nanoindentation on the sintered sample using a Berkovich tip with a maximum load of 10 mN and a dwell time of 10 seconds. Compare the hardness values of the sintered sample against a control sample of the same composition processed via SPS at 1100°C (where grain growth and HCP formation are expected) and a control sample of pure FCC CoCrFeNi (without Ti) processed under identical sintering conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the hardness of the sintered CoCrFeNiTi sample is statistically indistinguishable from the pure FCC CoCrFeNi control sample (indicating solute strengthening from Ti is negligible or absent) OR if the hardness is significantly lower than the cast baseline (indicating failure to densify or formation of a soft phase) OR if XRD analysis reveals >10% HCP phase content despite the rapid sintering protocol.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. This paper reports the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a low-density Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Prior to sintering, the morphology, chemical homogeneity and crystal structures of the powders were thoroughly investigated by varying the milling times to find optimal conditions for densification. The sintered bulk RHEAs were produced with diverse feedstock powder conditions. The microstructural development of the materials was analyzed in terms of phase composition and constitution, chemical homogeneity, and crystallographic properties. Hardness and elastic constants also were measured. The calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) was performed to predict the phase changes in the alloy, and the results were compared with the experiments. Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
